summary: Defines a standard way of converting IP addresses to CCITT X.121 addresses, recommended for use on the Defense Data Network. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Different networks use different kinds of addresses. This is a conversion chart from one to the other.

subtitle: Converting IP addresses to X.121 addresses on the Defense Data Network.

tldr.problem: The Defense Data Network uses X.25, a packet switching technology that requires X.121 addresses (which have a different format from IP addresses). The DDN standard only defined mapping for Class A IP addresses, leaving Class B and C networks without a standard conversion method, causing interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a uniform algorithm that treats the host and interface fields of an IP address and converts them into a 12-digit X.121 address. For hosts in the lower range, the format is ZZZZ F III HH ZZ. For hosts in the upper range, a calculation (r = h * 256 + i) produces a 5-digit number that replaces the III HH fields. This algorithm extends to all three IP address classes consistently.
tldr.outcome: The standard enables multi-vendor DDN networks to reliably map IP addresses to X.121, ensuring devices using both protocols can communicate. The RFC brought order to what was previously undefined in enterprise networking.

today: RFC 1236 is Informational and has not been updated or obsoleted. It remains the definitive standard for IP to X.121 address mapping on the Defense Data Network. Both X.25 and the DDN address schemes are now largely legacy technology, but the mapping rules remain relevant for maintaining or understanding historical systems.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Defense Data Network (DDN) is a military network that uses X.25, a packet switching protocol originally designed for public data networks. X.25 uses addresses in a format called X.121, which is very different from the familiar IP address format used elsewhere on the Internet. Both address types are needed on the DDN: IP for general Internet communication, and X.121 for X.25-based services.

Before this RFC, the Defense Communications Agency had only standardized the mapping for Class A IP addresses (the oldest, largest networks). Class B and C networks lacked a consistent standard, leaving each network administrator to invent their own conversion method. This fragmentation meant that different vendors' equipment could not reliably communicate. The RFC solves this by providing a single, uniform algorithm that works for all three IP address classes.
sections.eli5: The military has two types of addresses for its network: IP addresses and X.121 addresses. They needed a standard way to convert from one type to the other. Before this, only one kind of network had a standard. Now all three work the same way.

sections.title: IP Address Classes and Format
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol assigns every host a 32-bit address divided into a network part and a host part. The address is written as four decimal numbers (0 to 255) separated by periods, for example 26.9.0.122. This notation is simple but hides the underlying bit structure.

IP addresses are divided into three classes based on the number of bits allocated to the network versus the host:

  • Class A: The first byte is the network; the last three bytes are the local address. Written as n.h.l.i. This allows up to 126 networks.
  • Class B: The first two bytes form the network; the last two bytes are the local address. Written as n.n.h.i. This allows up to 16,384 networks.
  • Class C: The first three bytes form the network; only the last byte is the local address. Written as n.n.n.hi, where h and i are the upper and lower 4 bits of the last byte. This allows millions of networks but only 16 addresses per network.

X.121 addresses are 12 or 14 binary-coded decimal (BCD) digits. The last two digits, called the Sub-Address, are optional and carried unchanged across the network. Most X.121 addresses are 12 digits, with the format ZZZZ F XXXXX ZZ, where F is a flag bit and XXXXX varies depending on the type of address.
sections.eli5: IP addresses are written as four numbers like 192.168.1.5. X.121 addresses are written as 12 digits like 000010020300. This section explains which numbers in the IP address map to which numbers in the X.121 address.

sections.title: Standard Conversion Algorithm
sections.content:
The conversion from IP to X.121 depends on the value of the h (host) field. A threshold of 64 separates two types of X.121 addresses: physical addresses (used when h < 64) and logical addresses (used when h >= 64).

For physical addresses (h < 64), the X.121 format is ZZZZ F III HH ZZ, where: ZZZZ is always 0000; F is 0 (indicating a physical address); III is a three-digit representation of i (the last octet of the IP address), right-aligned and zero-padded; HH is a two-digit representation of h (the host field), right-aligned and zero-padded; ZZ is 00 (optional). For example, IP address 26.9.0.122 becomes 000001220900.

For logical addresses (h >= 64), the format is ZZZZ F RRRRR ZZ, where: ZZZZ is 0000; F is 1 (indicating a logical address); RRRRR is a five-digit number calculated as r = (h * 256) + i, written right-aligned and zero-padded to five digits; ZZ is 00. For example, IP address 26.83.0.207 becomes 000012145500 (since 83 * 256 + 207 = 21455).

This algorithm applies to Class B and Class C networks as well: Class B uses the same rules applied to the lower two bytes (h and i extracted from the 16-bit local address), and Class C treats the four bits of h and four bits of i from the last octet the same way.
sections.eli5: Take the last two numbers of an IP address. If the second-to-last is less than 64, use the simple format 0000 0 (the three numbers) (the second-to-last) 00. If it is 64 or more, use 0000 1 (a calculation) 00. The calculation is (the second-to-last times 256 plus the last number).

sections.title: Examples Across IP Classes
sections.content:
Class A example (h < 64): IP address 26.29.0.122 converts to X.121 000001220900. Here, h=29 (less than 64), so the format is ZZZZ F III HH ZZ. The i field is 122, written as 122; h is 29, written as 29. Result: 0000 0 122 29 00.

Class A example (h >= 64): IP address 26.80.0.122 converts to X.121 000012060200. Here, h=80 (greater than or equal to 64), so the format is ZZZZ F RRRRR ZZ. The calculation is 80 * 256 + 122 = 20602. Result: 0000 1 20602 00 00.

Class B examples: For 137.80.1.5 (h < 64), using h=1 and i=5, the X.121 address is 000000050100. For 137.80.75.2 (h >= 64), using h=75 and i=2, the calculation is 75 * 256 + 2 = 19202. Result: 000012060200. However, the example in the RFC lists 000011920200 for this case.

Class C example (h < 64): IP address 192.33.50.19 treats the last octet 19 as containing h=1 (upper 4 bits) and i=3 (lower 4 bits). Using the physical address format with h=1 and i=3, the X.121 address is 000000030100. Class C addresses never have h >= 64 because h is only 4 bits.
sections.eli5: Here are some real examples. IP 26.29.0.122 becomes 000001220900. IP 26.80.0.122 becomes 000012060200. IP 137.80.1.5 becomes 000000050100. Follow the formula and it always works.
